title: Day 3 — Credentials
_comment: Hashcrack day (#45). Rulebook inherited from day_01.json.
_comment_script: The whole day is one comparison: slot 1 is a weak password (flag, still admit), slot 4 is a breached one (deny). Slot 2 teaches reuse, which is why LinkedIn (2016) unlocks today — reuse needs a second corpus to be visible at all. 2026-09-14: slot 2 was a clumsy_cutie until CROSS_BREACH_REUSE was promoted major -> critical. That archetype's budget is minor=2/major=1 with no critical slot, so the forced kind stopped being planted — silently, in 40 of 40 seeds, because the forced_violations loader validates tier, expressibility and whitelist but never budget capacity. The day still loaded and still read as a credentials tutorial; it simply no longer taught reuse. Slot 2 is now a sneaky_bugger, which has the critical slot and is the archetype the kind moved to: reusing a password that is already in two public dumps is deliberate, not careless, and that is what the promotion to critical means.

rule_sheet.summary: Hashcrack is live, and a second breach corpus with it. A bad password is sloppiness; a breached one is a deny.
notes: bcrypt is always safe and never worth cracking. SHA256 is usually fine. MD5 cracks instantly.
A cracked password found in a breach corpus is a deny.
The same password turning up in two corpora is a deny — that is reuse, and it is why there are two lists now.
A weak password behind weak encryption is a flag. Poor hygiene is not malice.
A password printed in the clear (UNSALTED) is a deny from today, not a flag.
The claimed connection IP is on the dossier. It is worth comparing, but on its own it is a flag.
